title: Parmjit Parmar Got Five Years for a $212 Million Fraud — and His Co-Conspirators Are Still on the Run
excerpt: The Colts Neck executive built a phantom healthcare empire with fake banks, fake customers, and a London listing. A New Jersey court just closed one chapter — but the real story is far from over.
body:
On May 8, a federal judge in New Jersey sentenced Parmjit "Paul" Parmar, the 55-year-old former CEO of Constellation Healthcare Technologies, to five years in prison — the maximum allowed under his plea agreement — for masterminding a securities fraud scheme that defrauded investors of $212.5 million. He was also ordered to pay $125 million in restitution.

The sentence caps a seven-year saga that began when Constellation, a London-listed healthcare revenue-cycle management company, collapsed spectacularly in late 2017 after auditors discovered that its financial statements were almost entirely fabricated.

## The Architecture of a Phantom Empire

Parmar's scheme was breathtaking in its audacity. Between 2015 and 2017, he created fake subsidiary companies, fabricated bank statements, invented phantom customers, and inflated Constellation's revenue from virtually nothing to over $100 million on paper. The goal: to convince a New York-based private equity firm to take the company private at a vastly inflated valuation.

It worked — for a while. The private equity firm invested $212.5 million based on financials that were, according to prosecutors, "almost entirely fictitious." Parmar used portions of the funds to service earlier fraudulent debts, pay co-conspirators, and fund a lavish lifestyle that included a mansion in Colts Neck, New Jersey — a property that has since been foreclosed.

## The Unravelling

The fraud unravelled in late 2017 when the acquiring firm's auditors began examining Constellation's books more closely and found discrepancies that could not be explained. Within months, the company filed for bankruptcy, wiping out both equity and debt investors.

Parmar was arrested in 2018 and pleaded guilty in 2020 to one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud. His sentencing was delayed repeatedly — in part because investigators were pursuing his co-conspirators, CFO Sotirios "Sam" Zaharis and corporate secretary Ravi Chivukula, both of whom remain fugitives.

## The Diaspora Lens

For Indian Americans in corporate leadership, the Parmar case is an uncomfortable mirror. At its peak, Constellation was held up as a success story — an Indian-origin entrepreneur taking a healthcare services company global through a London listing. The collapse shattered that narrative and raised uncomfortable questions about due diligence in cross-border transactions involving diaspora executives.

The case also highlights a pattern that federal prosecutors have flagged with increasing frequency: healthcare fraud by executives who exploit the sector's complexity to fabricate revenue streams that are difficult for outside investors to verify.

Parmar's co-conspirators remain at large. The $125 million restitution order is largely symbolic — the money is gone, and the investors who lost it are unlikely to recover more than pennies on the dollar.

**What to watch:** The DOJ's pursuit of Zaharis and Chivukula continues. If either is apprehended, their trials could reveal the full extent of the network that enabled a $212 million fraud to pass undetected for years.
